_comment: Rules that read the code rather than the text of it. Each carries one tree-sitter query per language, so teaching a rule about another language is an entry here rather than a change in Rust. What a query cannot express is judgment — whether the argument is a literal, which decides between an ugly call and a dangerous one — and that lives in ast.rs where it can be tested. Captures: @hit is what gets reported, @arg is the argument judged for literalness.

rules.title: Code is built at run time and executed
rules.description: A value decided while the app is running is handed to something that executes it as code.
rules.impact: If any part of that value can be influenced from outside, whoever influences it chooses what the app does next.
rules.fix: Work out what the code is actually for. A lookup table, a match on a fixed set of names, or a small parser will do the job without running text as code.

rules.title: A disallowed hash function is used
rules.description: MD5 or SHA-1 is used as a hash function. Both have practical collision attacks, and approved-hash rules disallow them for any cryptographic use.
rules.impact: Anything that relies on the hash to tell two things apart, or to prove something was not changed, can be fooled by somebody who builds a second input with the same hash. Used for passwords, both are also fast enough to guess through quickly.
rules.fix: Use SHA-256 or stronger for integrity and signatures, and a password hashing function (Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt) for passwords. If this hash is only a cache key or a file checksum with no security purpose, say so where it is used; Python lets you pass usedforsecurity=False.

rules.title: A cipher or block mode that is not approved is used
rules.description: Data is encrypted with ECB, the block mode that encrypts equal blocks to equal output, or with a retired cipher such as DES, triple DES, RC4, RC2 or Blowfish.
rules.impact: ECB leaves the shape of the data visible through the encryption, and the retired ciphers can be broken or have known practical attacks, so the encrypted data is less private than it looks.
rules.fix: Use AES with GCM (or ChaCha20-Poly1305) through your language's high-level library, which chooses the mode and the nonce for you. In Java, always name the mode: Cipher.getInstance("AES") quietly means ECB.
rules.looksFor: encryption in ECB mode, or with a retired cipher such as DES, triple DES, RC4, RC2, or Blowfish

rules.title: Data is encrypted in a way that does not show whether it was changed
rules.description: Data is encrypted with a block mode that keeps it secret but cannot tell when it has been altered: CBC, CTR, CFB, or OFB. Someone who can change the encrypted data can often change what it decrypts to, without knowing the key.
rules.impact: Encrypted data that is stored or sent somewhere a person can reach, such as a cookie, a token, or a file, can be tampered with, and the app will decrypt and trust the altered result. With CBC, error messages about padding can also let somebody decrypt it bit by bit.
rules.fix: Use an authenticated mode: AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, or a library that does it for you (Fernet, libsodium's secretbox, Tink). If this code already signs the encrypted data with a separate HMAC and checks it before decrypting, it is correct as it is: this rule sees one call at a time and cannot see the HMAC, which is why it is only ever a finding and never a clean result.
rules.looksFor: encryption in CBC, CTR, CFB, or OFB mode, which keeps data secret but does not show whether it was changed; only ever a finding, because a separate HMAC elsewhere can make it correct

rules.title: The app redirects to a destination built from a value
rules.description: A redirect sends the user to a destination that is built from a value rather than written out or produced from the app's own routes.
rules.impact: If the destination comes from the request, as a ?next= parameter usually does, a link on the app's own domain can send somebody to a lookalike sign-in page on another domain, and the address they clicked was genuine.
rules.fix: Redirect only to the app's own routes, built with its router (url_for, reverse, a Rails _path helper), or check the destination against a short list of allowed hosts. For a return-to address, accept only a path that starts with a single / and not //.

rules.title: A WebSocket address without encryption is written into the code
rules.description: A `ws://` address to another computer is written into the code. `ws://` is a WebSocket with no encryption, the way `http://` is a page without it.
rules.impact: Everything sent over the connection, including the session it was opened with and whatever the person types, can be read and changed by anybody on the network between them and the app: the same café Wi-Fi, a compromised router.
rules.fix: Use `wss://`. In a browser, build the address from the page's own, so it follows the page to HTTPS: `(location.protocol === 'https:' ? 'wss://' : 'ws://') + location.host + '/socket'`.

rules.title: A signature is compared in a way that leaks how much of it was right
rules.description: A keyed signature (an HMAC, the kind a webhook or a signed link carries) is checked with an ordinary equals comparison. An ordinary comparison stops at the first character that differs, so it is not constant-time: it takes slightly longer the more of the signature is right.
rules.impact: Someone who can send many guesses and time the answers can work out a valid signature one character at a time, and then forge the requests the signature was meant to prove came from you or your partner.

rules.title: A sign-in token is allowed to say where the key that checks it comes from
rules.description: The code reads, from a signed token (such as a JWT) it has not yet checked, where its key is to come from: the `jku` header (the address of a set of keys), `x5u` (the address of a certificate), or `jwk` (the key itself), and hands that straight to something that fetches a key or makes one. rules.impact: Anybody can make a key of their own, sign a token saying they are any user or an admin, and point the token at their own key: the app fetches it, the signature checks out, and they are in. A `jku` or `x5u` address also makes the app fetch whatever address an outsider writes.
rules.fix: Take keys only from your sign-in server's own address, written in your settings, never from the token: for example `PyJWKClient(JWKS_URL)` in Python, `createRemoteJWKSet(new URL(JWKS_URL))` with `jose` or `jwksClient({ jwksUri: JWKS_URL })` in Node.js, and choose the key from that set by the token's `kid`. Ignore `jku`, `x5u`, and `jwk` in the token. If the app must follow them, compare the whole address with a fixed list of your sign-in server's addresses before fetching anything; if this line already comes after such a check, the finding is wrong, and `sv review` can record that.

rules.title: A sign-in token is written where the page's scripts can read it
rules.description: The page's own code writes a value under a name that says it is a sign-in token (`token`, `jwt`, `accessToken`, `refresh`) into `localStorage` or `sessionStorage`, or into a cookie set from the page, which can never be `HttpOnly`.

Let the server hold the session and give the browser an `HttpOnly` cookie, set by the server, or put a backend-for-frontend between the page and the sign-in provider so tokens never reach the page. If a token must be in the page, keep a short-lived access token in memory only, never the refresh token.

rules.title: An account is found, or a sign-in recorded, by the email address the sign-in provider sent
rules.description: After someone signs in through another service ("Sign in with Google", GitHub, Microsoft, or any OpenID Connect provider), the code finds their account by the email address that service sent, such as `userinfo["email"]`, `profile.emails[0].value`, `auth.info.email`, `oidcUser.getEmail()`, or `info.Principal.FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.Email)`, or records that address as who is signed in (`session["user"] = userinfo["email"]`), rather than the provider's own id for the person (`sub`).
rules.impact: An email address can pass from one person to another: a work address reused after someone leaves, or a provider that lets people choose theirs. Whoever holds the address next signs in to the first person's account and sees everything in it. A provider marking the address verified does not change this; it says the address works, not that it belongs to the same person.
rules.fix: Store the provider's `sub` (with the provider's name, if there is more than one) when the account is made, and find the account by that pair on every sign-in. Keep the email address only for writing to people. If you link a provider's sign-in to an account that already exists with the same email address on purpose, ask the person to sign in the old way first and confirm the link.

rules.title: A check answers "yes" when it fails
rules.description: A function whose name says it checks something (verify, validate, authorize, check, allow, permission, guard, and the like) answers "yes" from its error handler: `except: return True`, `catch (e) { return true; }`, `rescue … true`, an Express check that calls `next()` from its `catch`, Go's `if err != nil { return true }`, Rust's `.unwrap_or(true)` or `Err(_) => true`, or a shell function's `|| return 0`.
rules.impact: When the check itself breaks (a token it cannot read, a database that is down, a signature it cannot work out), the app goes ahead as if the check had passed. Whoever can make the check throw, often just by sending something malformed, gets past it.
rules.fix: Make the error handler answer "no": return false, raise the error, or pass it on (`next(err)` in Express), and log what went wrong. If an error really should let the person through, write down why next to the code, and say so to whoever reads this finding.
